question: Under Section 475.278(1)(b), F.S., what is the presumed default brokerage relationship for a Florida licensee working with a customer, absent a written agreement establishing a different relationship?
choice_c: Dual agent with full fiduciary duties to both parties
explanation: Section 475.278(1)(b), F.S., presumes that all Florida licensees operate as transaction brokers unless a single agent or no brokerage relationship is established in writing with a customer -- the transaction broker relationship is Florida's statutory default.

question: A transaction broker under Section 475.278(2), F.S., owes the customer which of the following duties?
choice_a: Dealing honestly and fairly, accounting for funds, using skill/care/diligence, disclosing material facts, presenting offers/counteroffers in a timely manner, and maintaining limited confidentiality
choice_b: Full fiduciary duties identical to those owed by a single agent, including undivided loyalty
choice_c: No duties whatsoever, since a transaction broker owes nothing to either party
choice_d: A duty to always recommend the highest possible purchase price to the buyer
explanation: Section 475.278(2), F.S., defines a transaction broker's duties as dealing honestly and fairly, accounting for all funds, exercising skill, care, and diligence, disclosing known material facts, presenting all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner, and limited confidentiality -- a narrower, non-fiduciary set of duties than a single agent owes.

question: Florida's transaction broker limited confidentiality duty specifically does NOT protect which two categories of information from disclosure to the other party, absent a party's request otherwise?
choice_a: The buyer's Social Security number and the seller's bank account number
choice_b: That a buyer is willing to pay more than the offered price, or that a seller is willing to accept less than the asking price
choice_c: The physical square footage and lot size of the property
explanation: Under Florida's transaction broker limited confidentiality duty, certain information is specifically excluded from protection unless a party gives written direction otherwise -- notably, that a buyer is willing to pay more than the price offered, or that a seller is willing to accept less than the asking price, along with the motivation for buying or selling and any facts a party specifically instructs the licensee to disclose.
source_note: Section 475.278(2), F.S. (Transaction Broker -- limited confidentiality exceptions)

question: A single agent relationship under Section 475.278(3), F.S., requires the licensee to owe the represented party which set of duties?
choice_a: Only the limited duties owed by a transaction broker
choice_b: No duty of confidentiality of any kind
choice_c: The traditional fiduciary duties, including loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, full disclosure, accounting, skill/care/diligence, and presenting offers in a timely manner
choice_d: A duty to represent both the buyer and seller equally at all times
explanation: Section 475.278(3)(a), F.S., establishes that a single agent owes the party represented the traditional fiduciary duties: loyalty, confidentiality, obedience, full disclosure, accounting, and the exercise of skill, care, and diligence, along with timely presentation of offers and disclosure of known material facts -- a full undivided-loyalty relationship, unlike a transaction broker.

question: Disclosure of a single agent relationship to a customer must occur, per Section 475.278(3)(b)1., F.S.:
choice_a: Only after the transaction has closed
choice_b: Only if the customer specifically requests written disclosure
choice_c: Never -- single agent relationships require no disclosure at all
choice_d: Before, or at the time of, entering into a listing agreement or an agreement for representation, or before the showing of property, whichever occurs first
explanation: Section 475.278(3)(b)1., F.S., requires a single agent to disclose that relationship before, or at the time of, entering into a listing agreement or agreement for representation, or before the showing of property, whichever occurs first -- ensuring the customer understands the nature of the relationship at the earliest meaningful point.

question: A broker representing a seller as a single agent who wishes to transition to a transaction broker relationship for that same customer must:
choice_a: Obtain the customer's written consent, using a proper transition disclosure
choice_b: Simply notify the customer verbally with no documentation required
choice_c: Automatically transition with no consent or disclosure needed
choice_d: Wait until after closing to make the change
explanation: Section 475.278(3)(b)2., F.S., requires that a single agent transitioning to a transaction broker relationship for the same customer obtain the customer's prior written consent using the statutorily prescribed transition disclosure -- protecting the customer from an unnoticed loss of full fiduciary representation.
source_note: Section 475.278(3)(b)2., F.S. (Single Agent to Transaction Broker Transition)

question: Under a 'no brokerage relationship' with a party under Section 475.278(4)(a), F.S., the licensee owes only which limited duties?
choice_a: Full fiduciary duties identical to a single agent
choice_b: Dealing honestly and fairly, disclosing known material facts affecting the value of residential real property not readily observable to the buyer, and accounting for all funds entrusted
choice_c: No duties of any kind, since no relationship exists
choice_d: A duty to negotiate the lowest possible price on the customer's behalf
explanation: Section 475.278(4)(a), F.S., establishes that a licensee with no brokerage relationship to a party still owes limited duties: dealing honestly and fairly, disclosing known material facts affecting residential property value that are not readily observable, and accounting for funds entrusted to the licensee.

question: Disclosure of a 'no brokerage relationship' status must occur, per Section 475.278(4)(b), F.S.:
choice_a: Only if the buyer later files a lawsuit
explanation: Section 475.278(4)(b), F.S., requires disclosure of a 'no brokerage relationship' before the showing of property, so a customer understands from the outset that the licensee is not representing their interests in the transaction.

question: The 'designated sales associate' relationship under Section 475.2755, F.S., allowing different associates within the same brokerage to act as single agents for opposing parties in the same transaction, is limited to circumstances where:
choice_a: Any residential sale, regardless of the parties' assets
choice_b: Only commercial leasing transactions, with no asset threshold
choice_c: Any transaction where the brokerage employs more than 5 associates
choice_d: The transaction is not a residential sale, and both the buyer and seller have assets of $1 million or more
explanation: Section 475.2755, F.S., restricts the designated sales associate option to non-residential transactions where both the buyer and seller have assets of $1 million or more -- a narrow carve-out for sophisticated commercial parties, not available in an ordinary residential sale.

question: Designated sales associates under Section 475.2755, F.S., each owe their respective customer the duties of:
choice_a: A single agent, per Section 475.278(3), F.S.
choice_d: No duty at all, since the broker (not the associates) holds all responsibility
explanation: Under the designated sales associate structure, each designated associate owes their own customer the full single agent duties set out in Section 475.278(3), F.S., even though both associates operate under the same supervising broker in the same transaction.

question: A customer may terminate a broker relationship (e.g., cancel a listing agreement or buyer representation agreement) generally in accordance with:
choice_a: No process at all -- brokerage relationships in Florida can never be terminated once formed
choice_b: The specific termination provisions in the written agreement between the parties
choice_c: A mandatory 1-year minimum term set by FREC for every listing agreement
choice_d: Verbal notice only, with no reference to the written agreement
explanation: Termination of a brokerage relationship is generally governed by the specific terms of the written listing or representation agreement between broker and customer, which typically addresses cancellation rights, notice requirements, and any protection period for procuring cause after termination.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section III.H (Terminating Broker Relationship)

question: The Florida Brokerage Relationship Disclosure Act, establishing single agent, transaction broker, and no brokerage relationship categories, is codified at:
explanation: The Brokerage Relationship Disclosure Act -- which created Florida's transaction broker, single agent, and no brokerage relationship framework -- is codified at Sections 475.2701 through 475.2801, F.S.

question: A broker who accepts a listing agreement granting the exclusive right to sell a property is entitled to a commission:
choice_a: Only if the listing broker personally locates the buyer
choice_b: Never, since exclusive right of sale listings never earn a commission
choice_c: Only if the seller personally sells the property to a family member
choice_d: If the property sells during the listing term, regardless of who actually procures the buyer
explanation: Under an exclusive right of sale listing agreement, the listing broker earns a commission if the property sells during the listing term regardless of who procures the buyer -- including if the seller finds the buyer independently -- distinguishing it from an exclusive agency listing, where the seller retains the right to sell without owing a commission if the seller personally procures the buyer.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section IV.A-B (Listing Agreements; Entitlement to Commission)

question: The doctrine allowing a broker to claim entitlement to a commission where the broker was the 'procuring cause' of a sale addresses situations where:
choice_a: A dispute arises over which of two or more brokers actually brought about the ultimate sale, and therefore is entitled to the commission
choice_b: The buyer defaults on the mortgage after closing
choice_c: The seller unilaterally decides not to pay any commission for any reason
choice_d: The property fails a home inspection
explanation: Procuring cause doctrine resolves commission disputes between brokers by asking which broker's uninterrupted efforts were the predominating cause of bringing about the sale -- a common issue when a buyer works with multiple agents or a listing expires and the buyer later purchases through a different agent.
source_note: General real estate commission/procuring cause doctrine, well-corroborated across state real estate law

question: A licensee assisting a customer with legal aspects of a transaction, such as explaining the general effect of a warranty deed versus a quitclaim deed, must be careful not to:
choice_a: Ever mention the existence of different deed types to a customer
choice_b: Engage in the unauthorized practice of law by drafting legal documents or giving legal advice reserved for attorneys
choice_c: Recommend that a customer consult an attorney for complex legal questions
choice_d: Explain any general real estate concept whatsoever
explanation: While licensees routinely explain general real estate concepts and use standardized, association-approved forms, drafting original legal documents or giving legal advice beyond the scope of general market/practice knowledge risks the unauthorized practice of law -- a recurring risk area the broker exam content outline flags under Legal Titles, Deeds, etc.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section III.I (Legal -- Titles, Deeds, etc.); Section 454.23, F.S. (unauthorized practice of law)

question: A warranty deed differs from a quitclaim deed primarily in that a warranty deed:
choice_a: Can only be used for commercial property
choice_c: Includes covenants warranting the grantor's clear title, while a quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor may have, with no warranties
explanation: A warranty deed includes the grantor's covenants warranting good, clear title against claims, offering the grantee stronger legal protection, while a quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest (if any) the grantor actually holds, with no warranty of title -- commonly used to clear up a title defect or between family members rather than in an arm's-length sale.
source_note: General Florida real property conveyance principles, Chapter 689, F.S.; well-corroborated real estate practice knowledge

question: An exclusive agency listing agreement, as distinguished from an exclusive right of sale listing, permits the seller to:
choice_a: Owe a commission to the listing broker no matter who sells the property, including the seller personally
choice_b: Cancel the listing at any time with no notice required
choice_c: List the property with multiple brokers simultaneously under the same exclusive agreement
choice_d: Sell the property personally without owing the listing broker a commission, while still owing a commission if any other agent procures the buyer
explanation: Under an exclusive agency listing, the seller retains the right to sell the property personally without owing the listing broker a commission, but still owes the broker a commission if any other agent (including a cooperating broker) procures the buyer -- a middle ground between an exclusive right of sale and an open listing.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section IV.A (Listing Agreements)
